title: Primitives versus objects (and why typeof lies)
hook: JavaScript stores seven primitive kinds and everything else is an object. Primitives copy by value; objects alias by reference — and `typeof` does not always tell you which one you have.

blocks.text: A **primitive** is an immutable value stored directly — not a pointer to something else. JavaScript has seven primitives: `undefined`, `null`, `boolean`, `number`, `bigint`, `string`, and `symbol`. Everything else — plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, regular expressions — is an **object** (a collection of properties on the heap). When you assign a primitive, JavaScript copies the bits. When you assign an object, JavaScript copies the reference, so two variables can point at the same object.

entries.plainDefinition: An immutable atomic value — undefined, null, boolean, number, bigint, string, or symbol. Assigned by copy.
entries.example: `let a = 42; let b = a;` — `b` gets its own copy of 42.

entries.plainDefinition: A mutable collection of key–value properties on the heap. Assignment copies the reference, not the contents.
entries.example: `const a = { x: 1 }; const b = a; b.x = 2;` — `a.x` is also 2.

entries.plainDefinition: A temporary object (`new String('hi')`) that boxes a primitive so you can call methods. Prefer primitives; avoid `new String()`.
entries.example: `'hello'.toUpperCase()` — engine auto-boxes the string primitive briefly.

entries.plainDefinition: Returns a string label for a value's type. Famous bug: `typeof null` returns `'object'` for historical reasons.

blocks.text: Confusing copy and alias causes real bugs. You pass a config object to two functions; one mutates `config.timeout` and the other sees the change because they share the same reference. You compare two arrays with `===` and get `false` even when contents match — `===` compares references, not deep structure. In C#, value types copy and reference types alias — same mental model, but JavaScript only has primitives (copy) and objects (alias); there is no `struct` keyword.

blocks.title: Quick picker
blocks.body: Counters and math → `number` or `bigint`. Text → `string`. Unique keys → `symbol`. Yes/no → `boolean`. Missing value → `undefined` (uninitialized) or `null` (intentional empty). Collections and entities → plain objects and arrays.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Primitives live in the variable slot
items.body: `let count = 10` stores the number 10 directly. `let copy = count` duplicates the value — changing `copy` does not affect `count`.

items.title: Objects live on the heap; variables hold references
items.body: `const user = { name: 'Ada' }` stores a reference. `const alias = user` points at the same object — mutations are shared.

items.title: Primitives are immutable
items.body: You cannot change a string in place. `'hi' + '!'` creates a new string. Object properties can be added, changed, or deleted.

items.title: Auto-boxing for method calls
items.body: `'hello'.length` briefly wraps the primitive in a `String` object, calls `.length`, then discards the wrapper. Do not use `new String()` yourself.

snippet.label: All seven primitives
snippet.code:
let missing;              // undefined — declared, no value
const empty = null;       // null — intentional "no object"
const flag = true;        // boolean
const price = 19.99;      // number (IEEE 754 double)
const bigId = 9007199254740993n; // bigint — arbitrary precision integer
const name = 'Ada';       // string — immutable text
const secret = Symbol('token'); // symbol — unique identity
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `undefined` is the default for uninitialized `let`/`var`. Line 2: `null` is an intentional empty reference (still typeof `'object'` — see topic 2). Line 4: all JS numbers are doubles — same family of imprecision as C# `double`. Line 5: `bigint` needs the `n` suffix. Line 7: `symbol` creates a unique value — useful for object keys that won't collide.

snippet.label: Copy vs alias
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–4: number assignment copies the value. Lines 6–9: array assignment aliases — `push` on `list2` mutates `list1`. Lines 11–14: spread creates a new array shell; elements inside are still shared references (shallow copy).

snippet.label: typeof surprises
snippet.code:
console.log(typeof 42);           // 'number'
console.log(typeof 'hi');         // 'string'
console.log(typeof true);         // 'boolean'
console.log(typeof undefined);    // 'undefined'
console.log(typeof null);         // 'object' ← historical bug
console.log(typeof {});           // 'object'
console.log(typeof []);           // 'object' — arrays are objects
console.log(typeof function(){}); // 'function' — special case
snippet.explanation: Line 6: `typeof null === 'object'` is a well-known bug from the first JavaScript implementation — `null` was represented as a null pointer (type tag 0, ref 0). Line 8: arrays are objects; use `Array.isArray()` instead. Line 9: functions are callable objects; `typeof` returns `'function'` even though functions are objects.

blocks.title: Primitives and objects across languages
rows: Value types copy; reference types alias
Same runtime as JS; types are compile-time hints
`null` on reference types; value types use `Nullable<T>`

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `typeof null === 'object'` as proof that `null` is an object — it is a primitive. Comparing arrays or objects with `===` expecting deep equality. Creating wrapper objects with `new String('x')` — they break `===` comparisons with primitives. Assuming spread/destructuring is a deep clone — it is shallow.

blocks.text: In production, the primitive-vs-object distinction drives API design. Redis cache keys should be strings (primitives), not `String` objects. Configuration objects passed through middleware are aliased — clone defensively when immutability matters. `typeof null === 'object'` exists because the original Mocha engine used 32-bit tags where zero meant both `null` and empty object; fixing it would break old code. V8 stores small integers (Smi) inline and boxes larger numbers — but that is an engine detail, not the language spec. Interview signal: distinguish language semantics (copy vs alias) from engine optimizations.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: All numbers are IEEE 754 double — no int type
Cannot mix with `number` without explicit conversion
Each `Symbol()` is unique — `===` only true for same reference

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying `null` is an object because `typeof` says so. Claiming `===` does deep equality on arrays. Not knowing why `typeof null` is `'object'`. Using `new String()` in production code.

interviewTakeaways: Seven primitives: undefined, null, boolean, number, bigint, string, symbol. Everything else is an object.
Primitives copy on assignment; objects alias by reference.
`typeof null === 'object'` is a historical bug — `null` is a primitive.
60s: Primitives copy, objects alias. typeof null is object (bug). Seven primitives. Spread is shallow clone.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'null is an object because typeof says object.' Strong: 'null is a primitive; typeof bug from early engine tag bits.'
Using === for deep array/object equality — it compares references only.
Assuming destructuring or spread creates a deep clone — only the outer shell is new.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript adds compile-time types like `string` vs `String` — prefer lowercase primitives. `object` type excludes primitives; `Object` includes boxed wrappers.
C# splits `int`/`decimal`/`struct` (copy) from `class`/`string` (alias). JavaScript only has primitives (copy) and objects (alias) — no `decimal` or `struct`.
